title: The Data Science Process
description: The lifecycle of a data project, types of data and variables, tidy data, data quality and missingness, and how to formulate a question the data can answer.
overview: Data science is the practice of drawing useful conclusions from data. A model with a very good test score can still be useless if it answers the wrong question, is trained on data that do not represent the cases it will meet, or is built on a table whose columns mean something other than what the analyst thinks. Most of the effort of a real project, and most of its failures, lie before and after the modeling step: asking a precise question, understanding where the data came from, cleaning it, and checking whether the answer can be believed.

This chapter sets out the process and its vocabulary. It describes the stages of a project, the kinds of data and variables, the tidy table format that the rest of the book assumes, the problems that real data have (errors, duplicates, missing values), and the different kinds of question (describe, predict, infer, intervene) that call for different methods.
objectives: Describe the stages of a data science project and the questions asked at each.
Classify variables by measurement scale and decide which summaries and operations are meaningful.
Identify the unit of observation (granularity) of a table and put data in tidy form.
Recognize data quality problems and the three kinds of missing data (MCAR, MAR, MNAR).
Distinguish descriptive, predictive, inferential and causal questions, and explain how Simpson's paradox shows why the distinction matters.

sections.title: The lifecycle of a data project
body: A data project is less like a straight road and more like a loop. You start with a question, collect and clean data, look at it, build a model, test it, and discover that the question was not quite right or the data were not quite what you thought, so you go around again. Expect to go around many times, and expect most of the time to go into the data and the question, not the model. A data project goes through a cycle, usually many times.

list: **Question**: what decision or understanding is wanted, and how would we know we had it? What would be done differently depending on the answer?
**Data acquisition**: what data exist, who collected them, how, and for what purpose? Can we get more? Are we allowed to use them?
**Cleaning and preparation**: fix errors, handle missing values, join tables, and put the data in a usable form. This stage typically takes the largest share of the time.
**Exploration**: summarize, plot, look for patterns and anomalies, and check assumptions (the next chapters).
**Modeling and inference**: fit models, estimate quantities, test hypotheses, with a measure of uncertainty.
**Communication and action**: explain the findings and their limits to the people who must act on them; deploy a model if one was built.
**Monitoring**: check that the model or conclusion still holds as the world changes, and iterate.

body: The cycle is not a straight line. Exploration reveals problems with the data that send the analyst back to cleaning, and a poor result may show that the question was ill-posed. The standard industry description of the process is CRISP-DM (business understanding, data understanding, preparation, modeling, evaluation, deployment).

The Machine Learning book of this library covers the modeling stage in depth: choosing a model class, fitting it, and measuring its predictive performance. This book covers the stages around it, and the statistical thinking needed to judge what a result means: how the data were produced, how much a sample can tell us about a population, whether an observed difference is real, and whether an association is causal.

body.tip: Write the question down in one sentence, with the population it applies to, the quantity to be estimated or predicted, and what decision depends on it. Many projects fail because the question was never made precise, and the team optimizes a metric that no one cares about.

check.q: Which stage typically takes the largest share of effort in practice?
wrong: Fitting the final model
Writing the final report
Choosing the programming language

sections.title: Types of data and variables
body: Data differ in structure. **Structured** data fit a table with fixed columns (a spreadsheet, a database table). **Semi-structured** data have a flexible nested layout (JSON, XML, web logs). **Unstructured** data have no predefined schema: text, images, audio, video. Machine learning increasingly handles unstructured data by turning it into numeric vectors (embeddings), but analysis of most business and scientific data still starts from tables.
The columns of a table are **variables**, and what you can legitimately do with one depends on its measurement scale.

head: Scale
Meaning
Examples
Meaningful operations
rows: ordered categories, unequal or unknown gaps
order, median, percentiles; differences are not meaningful
differences, mean; ratios are not meaningful (20 °C is not 'twice as hot' as 10 °C)
equal differences and a true zero
table.caption: Scales of measurement.

list: A variable is **discrete** if it takes separated values (counts, categories) and **continuous** if it can take any value in a range (though measurement precision always makes it discrete in practice).
**Identifiers** (a customer id, a zip code) look numeric but are nominal: averaging zip codes is meaningless. Encoding them as numbers silently invites a model to treat 90210 as 'larger' than 10001.
**Dates and times** carry structure (day of week, season, elapsed time, time zone) that should be extracted explicitly, and they require care with time zones and daylight saving.
Ordinal variables are often analyzed as numbers (the mean satisfaction rating). That is a modeling assumption, that the gaps are roughly equal, and should be made knowingly.

example.title: Choosing a summary
example.problem: A survey asks 'How satisfied are you?' on a scale from 1 (very unhappy) to 5 (very happy). The answers of 7 people are 5, 4, 4, 1, 5, 5, 2. Which summaries are appropriate?
example.solution: The scale is ordinal. The median (4) and the distribution of counts (1: one person; 2: one; 4: two; 5: three) are safe. The mean, 3.71, is commonly reported and treats the gaps as equal, which may not be true. A nominal summary such as the mode (5) also works. The standard deviation depends on the equal-gap assumption as well.

check.q: A postal code stored as an integer is best treated as
wrong: a ratio variable
an interval variable
a continuous variable

check.q: Temperature in degrees Celsius is on which scale?
check.a: Interval: differences are meaningful, but there is no true zero
wrong: Ratio
Nominal
Ordinal

sections.title: Granularity and tidy data
body: Suppose a table has the columns customer, date, and amount. Does each row mean one purchase, one customer, or one customer per month? If you average the amount column without knowing, you may be averaging purchases when you meant customers, and the answer will be wrong. Before doing anything else, decide what one row stands for. The **unit of observation** (or **granularity**) of a table says what one row represents: one transaction, one customer, one customer-month, one patient visit. The granularity must be known before any analysis, because it decides what the columns mean and which comparisons are valid. A table with one row per transaction has an 'amount' column that can be summed; the same column in a table with one row per customer might be an average or a total. Aggregating to a coarser grain loses information and can change conclusions (see Simpson's paradox below).
**Tidy data** (Wickham) organizes a table so that

list: every **variable** is a column,
every **observation** is a row,
every type of observational unit has its own table.

body: Tidy tables make most analyses simple: filtering, grouping and plotting all assume it. Raw data are often **untidy**. A common case is the **wide** table in which the columns are values of a variable (one column per year), where the **long** form (columns year and value, one row per combination) is tidy.

head: country
table.caption: A wide table: the year is spread over the column names.

head: country
year
value
table.caption: The same data in tidy (long) form: three variables, six observations.

list: Each table should have a **primary key**: a column or combination of columns that uniquely identifies a row (here country and year). Checking that the key is unique is the first test of a dataset: duplicates silently inflate counts.
Keep a **data dictionary** that records the meaning, units, allowed values and source of each column. The numbers in a column labeled 'income' might be monthly, annual, before tax, or in thousands.
Data from different tables are linked by **keys** (joins), the subject of the SQL chapter.

check.q: In tidy data, each row is
check.a: one observation, with each variable in its own column
wrong: one variable, with each observation in its own column
one table
one file

sections.title: Data quality and missing data
body: Real data are never clean. Common problems:

list: **Errors and impossible values**: negative ages, a height of 2,000 cm, a date in the future. Often these are data entry mistakes or unit mix-ups (feet and meters). Sentinel values such as −999 or 0 used for 'unknown' are dangerous: a mean computed with them is nonsense.
**Duplicates**: the same record entered twice, or the same entity under different spellings ('Intl. Business Machines', 'IBM'). Duplicate entities across training and test sets cause leakage.
**Inconsistent formats**: dates as 03/04/2024 (March 4 or April 3?), mixed capitalization, trailing spaces, units.
**Outliers**: values far from the rest. They may be errors (remove or correct) or the most interesting observations (keep and study). Decide with domain knowledge, not by a mechanical rule.
**Measurement error and bias**: instruments drift, people misreport (underestimating alcohol use), definitions change over time.
**Selection**: the data may describe only part of the population (people who responded, customers who stayed, patients who came to the hospital).

body: Values are often missing, and //why// they are missing matters as much as how many. Rubin's taxonomy:

head: Mechanism
Meaning
Example
Consequence of dropping incomplete rows
rows: the chance of being missing is unrelated to anything
a lab sample is dropped by accident
loses data but does not bias results
the chance of being missing depends on other observed variables
older respondents skip an online question; age is recorded
bias can be corrected by modeling on the observed variables
the chance of being missing depends on the missing value itself
high earners refuse to report income
biased, and the bias cannot be fixed from the data alone
table.caption: Mechanisms of missingness.

list: **Deleting** rows with missing values (complete-case analysis) is simple and valid under MCAR, but wasteful and biased under MAR or MNAR.

**Imputation** fills in missing values: with the mean or median (simple, but it shrinks the variance and hides uncertainty), with predictions from other variables (regression, nearest neighbors), or with several plausible values (**multiple imputation**), which propagates the uncertainty.
Add an **indicator** for 'was missing', since missingness itself can be informative (a missing income field may correlate with default).
Always report how much data are missing, in which variables, and how it was handled.

example.title: Missingness biases an average
example.problem: A survey of 1000 people asks for income. True incomes average $50,000 for those who answer, and the 300 people with incomes above $100,000 (average $150,000) mostly decline to answer: only 60 of them respond. What is the average of the 760 responses, and what is the average income of all 1000 people?
example.solution: Respondents: 700 lower-income people at $50,000 each plus 60 high earners at $150,000. Mean = (700 × 50,000 + 60 × 150,000)/760 = (35,000,000 + 9,000,000)/760 = $57,900. Everyone: (700 × 50,000 + 300 × 150,000)/1000 = $80,000. The responses underestimate the true mean by 28%, and nothing in the responses alone reveals it: the data are MNAR.

check.q: High earners are less likely to report their income. This is
wrong: missing completely at random
missing at random given income
not missing data at all

sections.title: What kind of question is it?
body: Four kinds of question call for different methods, and mixing them up is a common source of wrong conclusions.

head: Kind
Question
Example
Typical methods
rows: average spending per customer last month
What will happen for a new case?
which customers will cancel next month
machine learning; judged by held-out accuracy
What can we say about a population from a sample?
is the average height of adults in a country between 165 and 170 cm?
What would happen if we changed something?
table.caption: Four kinds of questions.

body: A predictive model can be excellent without being causal. Ice cream sales predict drowning deaths (both rise with the temperature), but banning ice cream would not save lives. A **confounding variable** is a common cause of both the treatment and the outcome, and it makes associations misleading.
A trend present in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are combined.

example.title: Kidney stone treatments
example.problem: Two treatments for kidney stones had these success counts. Which is better?
solution: A is better for small stones and better for large stones, yet B looks better overall. The reason: doctors gave the more difficult, large-stone cases mostly to treatment A (263 of its 350 patients), and large stones have lower success rates for any treatment. Stone size is a **confounder**: it influences both which treatment is chosen and the outcome. The right comparison conditions on stone size, so A is better, assuming size is the only confounder (see Causal Inference).

body.h: Target population and the data you have

body: Every inference is about a **target population**, the group the conclusion is meant to describe. The data are a sample from a **sampling frame**, the list from which it was actually drawn. If they differ (an online survey of internet users to describe all adults), the conclusion holds for the sample's population only. A prediction model has a target population too: the cases it will see after deployment, which must resemble the training data. Writing down the unit of observation, the target population, the outcome and the time window before looking at any data prevents most errors, including **leakage** (using, to predict an outcome, information that would not be available at prediction time).

example.title: Defining a prediction task
example.problem: A hospital wants to predict readmission within 30 days. State the unit of observation, label and a feature that would leak.
example.solution: Unit: one hospital discharge (a patient with several discharges contributes several rows, so the split between training and test must be by patient). Label: whether the patient is readmitted within 30 days of discharge. Features: information available at discharge time. A leaking feature: 'total length of the follow-up appointments in the next month', which is known only after the discharge and itself depends on the readmission.

check.q: Simpson's paradox is the phenomenon that
check.a: a trend present in every subgroup can disappear or reverse in the combined data
wrong: averages are always larger than medians
adding data always reverses a conclusion
samples are always biased

check.a: Would reducing the price increase sales?
wrong: What were last month's sales?
Which customers are likely to buy?
Is the mean price different from 20?

quiz.q: A table has one row per purchase, with columns customer_id and amount. An analyst computes the mean of amount. What does this number estimate?
wrong: Average spend per customer
Average total spend per active customer
Average spend per customer per month
quiz.why: The mean averages over rows, and a row is one purchase. A per-customer average requires summing amounts by customer first, which changes the unit of observation.

quiz.q: For which variable is the statement "this value is twice that value" meaningful?
wrong: Temperature in °C
Calendar year
Satisfaction rating from 1 to 5
quiz.why: Only a ratio scale has a true zero, so ratios are meaningful. Income is ratio; Celsius temperature and calendar year are interval, and a rating is ordinal.

quiz.q: Why is reporting the mean of a 1-to-5 satisfaction rating a modeling assumption rather than a neutral summary?
quiz.a: It assumes the gaps between ratings are equal, which ordinal scales do not guarantee
wrong: Ratings are nominal, so they have no order and therefore no meaningful median either
A mean can be computed only for continuous variables, never for integer-valued ratings
The mean of integer-valued ratings must itself be an integer, which makes it misleading
quiz.why: Ordinal categories are ordered but the distance between 1 and 2 need not equal the distance between 4 and 5. The mean uses those distances; the median does not.

quiz.q: A table has columns store, Jan, Feb and Mar holding monthly sales for 4 stores. It is reshaped to tidy form with columns store, month and sales. How many rows does the tidy table have?
quiz.why: Tidy form has one row per store-month combination: 4 × 3 = 12. The month, which was spread across column names, becomes a variable.

quiz.q: A tidy table has columns country, year and value. What is the first sanity check on its primary key?
quiz.a: Each (country, year) pair appears exactly once
wrong: Each country appears exactly once
The year column is sorted in increasing order
The value column contains no repeated numbers
quiz.why: The key is the combination of columns that identifies a row. A country appears in many rows (one per year), so uniqueness of country alone is the wrong test; repeated key pairs signal duplicates that inflate counts.

quiz.q: A team trains a churn model with excellent test accuracy, but nobody uses it. Which cause does the chapter treat as most common in projects like this?
quiz.a: The question was never made precise enough to match a decision
wrong: The test set was too large for the accuracy estimate to be reliable
The model class was not flexible enough to fit the underlying data
Data cleaning consumed more time than modeling did, delaying the launch
quiz.why: A precise question states the population, the quantity predicted and the decision that depends on it. Without that, a project can optimize a metric no one cares about.

quiz.q: Why does the lifecycle end with monitoring instead of stopping at deployment?
quiz.a: The world changes, so a result that held at launch may stop holding
wrong: Monitoring replaces the need for held-out evaluation before launch
Deployed models must be retrained from scratch every single day
Monitoring is the stage at which missing values are first discovered
quiz.why: The data-generating process drifts over time. Checking that results still hold feeds the next pass around the cycle.

quiz.q: A lab technician accidentally spills 5% of the blood samples, chosen with no pattern. How should the missing results be classified, and what happens if those rows are dropped?
quiz.a: MCAR; some data are lost but no bias is introduced
wrong: MAR; the results are biased unless modeled on other variables
MNAR; the bias cannot be repaired from the data
MCAR; the mean of the remaining values is biased upward
quiz.why: When the chance of being missing is unrelated to anything, the remaining rows are still a representative subset. Only precision is lost.

quiz.q: Missing values in a column are replaced by the column mean. What is a main drawback?
quiz.a: It shrinks the variance and hides the uncertainty from missing values
wrong: It inflates the variance, because new values are added to the column
It removes the bias when the data are MNAR, since the mean is preserved
It shifts the column mean away from the mean of the observed values
quiz.why: Every filled-in value sits exactly at the center, so spread is understated and the filled values are treated as if they were real observations. The column mean itself is unchanged.

quiz.q: In a survey of 1000 people, 600 earn $40,000 and 400 earn $120,000. All 600 lower earners answer the income question, but only 100 of the high earners do. What is the mean of the responses?
quiz.why: (600 × 40,000 + 100 × 120,000)/700 = $51,429. The true mean is $72,000, so refusals tied to income itself (MNAR) bias the average downward. $80,000 is the unweighted average of the two incomes.

quiz.q: A column of ages uses −999 for "unknown". Nine rows have age 40 and one row has −999. A mean that ignores the convention gives what, in years?
quiz.why: (9 × 40 − 999)/10 = −639/10 = −63.9. A sentinel value is treated as a real measurement, so it must be converted to a missing marker before summarizing.

quiz.q: A column of company salaries contains one value of $9,000,000, far above the rest. What does the chapter recommend?
quiz.a: Use domain knowledge to judge whether it is an error or genuine
wrong: Delete any value more than three standard deviations from the mean
Always keep it, since removing data always introduces bias
Replace it with the column median before any analysis begins
quiz.why: An outlier may be a typo to correct or the most interesting case to study. A mechanical rule cannot tell these apart.

quiz.a: From 40 sampled units, is the mean lifetime of all units above 500 hours?
wrong: Among these same 40 units, what was the mean observed lifetime in hours?
Given this sample, will one particular unit last another 100 hours?
Would redesigning the cooling system lengthen the lifetime of units?
quiz.why: Inference generalizes from a sample to a population. The first alternative only describes the sample, the second predicts a single case, and the last asks about an intervention (causal).

quiz.q: Carrying matches predicts lung cancer well, and both are driven by smoking. Would a ban on carrying matches reduce lung cancer?
quiz.a: No: smoking is a confounder, and prediction does not show an intervention effect
wrong: Yes, because a predictor this accurate must reflect a real effect of matches
Yes, as long as the sample used to estimate the association is large enough
No, since an association between two variables is always entirely spurious
quiz.why: A confounder is a common cause of two variables and creates an association between them. Predictive accuracy says nothing about what would happen if one variable were changed.

quiz.q: Drug P has a higher success rate than drug Q among mild cases and also among severe cases, yet Q has the higher overall success rate. What is the most likely explanation?
quiz.a: Severity affected both which drug was given and the chance of success
wrong: Q is truly better, since the overall rate counts all of the patients together
The subgroup rates must contain a calculation error somewhere in the table
Rates computed from groups of different sizes can never be compared at all
quiz.why: This is Simpson's paradox. If P was given mostly to severe cases, which have lower success for any drug, its overall rate is dragged down even though it wins within each group.

quiz.q: Drug P succeeds in 9 of 10 mild cases and 30 of 100 severe cases. What is its overall success rate?
quiz.why: (9 + 30)/(10 + 100) = 39/110 = 35.5%. Averaging 90% and 30% to get 60% ignores that the groups have very different sizes.

quiz.q: An online poll of internet users is used to describe all adults in a country. The conclusion is justified for
quiz.a: the population of internet users who could be sampled, not for all adults
wrong: all adults, provided the number of responses is large
all adults, once missing answers are imputed
only the specific people who answered, not any larger group
quiz.why: Inference reaches only the population from which the sample was actually drawn. A larger sample from the same frame reduces random error but not this mismatch.

quiz.q: A model predicts whether a loan will default, using information known when the loan is approved. Which feature would leak?
quiz.a: The number of collection calls made after the loan went overdue
wrong: The applicant's income at application
The requested loan amount
The credit score at application
quiz.why: Collection calls only happen after a default is looming, so the feature is unavailable at prediction time and encodes the outcome itself.

summary: A data project cycles through question, data, cleaning, exploration, modeling, communication and monitoring. Precise questions and understanding of the data matter more than the model.
Variables are nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio; the scale limits the meaningful operations. Identifiers and codes are nominal even when numeric.
Know the unit of observation. Tidy data have one variable per column, one observation per row and one table per kind of unit; keys must be unique.
Data have errors, duplicates, outliers and bias. Missing data are MCAR, MAR or MNAR; dropping rows is valid only for MCAR, and MNAR cannot be repaired from the data alone.
Distinguish descriptive, predictive, inferential and causal questions. Confounders create Simpson's paradox, and conclusions hold only for the population the data represent.

problems.q: Classify each variable by scale: (a) shoe size in EU sizes, (b) the grade A/B/C/D, (c) the number of children, (d) the country of residence.
problems.solution: (a) interval or ordinal in practice (sizes are ordered with roughly equal steps, but zero is not meaningful); (b) ordinal; (c) ratio (a count with a true zero); (d) nominal.

problems.q: A table has one row per (customer, month) with columns customer_id, month and spend. What is its unit of observation and its primary key? What goes wrong if a row appears twice?
problems.solution: Unit: one customer in one month. Primary key: (customer_id, month). A duplicated row double-counts that month's spend, inflating totals and averages.
problems.a: A customer-month; key (customer_id, month); duplicates inflate sums.

problems.q: In a sample of 200, 40 values of 'blood pressure' are missing, all among patients who did not return for a follow-up visit. The remaining mean is 128. What can you say about the true mean, and what would you do?
problems.solution: The missingness depends on the follow-up behavior, which may be related to health status, so it is probably MAR or MNAR. The mean of 128 may be biased (patients who did not return might be healthier or sicker). Compare the observed characteristics of those with and without values, use the observed variables to impute (multiple imputation) or weight, and report the sensitivity of the conclusions.
problems.a: The complete-case mean may be biased; investigate the mechanism, impute with auxiliary variables, and report sensitivity.

problems.q: In the kidney stone example, compute the overall success rate of treatment A if it had been given to the same mix of stones as treatment B (270 small and 80 large out of 350).
problems.solution: A's rates are 93.1% (small) and 73.0% (large). With 270 small and 80 large: 0.931 × 270 + 0.730 × 80 = 251.4 + 58.4 = 309.8 out of 350 = 88.5%, above B's 82.6%. The reversal disappears when the groups have equal mix.
problems.a: About 88.5% for A versus 82.6% for B.

problems.q: Write a one-sentence question for a project on customer cancellation that states the unit, the population, the outcome and the time window.
problems.solution: For example: 'Among active subscribers on the first of each month, which will cancel before the end of that month, so that retention offers can be sent to the 10% most likely to cancel?'
problems.a: A sentence naming unit (subscriber-month), population (active subscribers), outcome (cancellation within the month) and use.
